title: "For developers"
description: "How the project is built — spec first, C++11 always, both platforms from one tree — and where to start hacking."

EOS Reimagined is a **spec-first** reimplementation. The Epic Online Services SDK's behavior was
reverse-engineered and written down *before* being rebuilt, so contributions start from an
understood contract rather than folklore: read the spec page for the thing you're touching, then
make the code match it, then prove it with tests on both platforms.

## The lay of the repository

| Path | What lives there |
|---|---|
| [`src/core/`](https://github.com/anishgoyal1108/EOS-Reimagined/tree/main/src/core) | The engine: platform/client singletons, callback manager, config, identity, tracer |
| [`src/interfaces/`](https://github.com/anishgoyal1108/EOS-Reimagined/tree/main/src/interfaces) | One file per implemented EOS interface (Lobby is the big one) |
| [`src/flat/`](https://github.com/anishgoyal1108/EOS-Reimagined/tree/main/src/flat) | The exported flat C ABI — thin trampolines over the interfaces |
| [`src/net/`](https://github.com/anishgoyal1108/EOS-Reimagined/tree/main/src/net) | The mesh: discovery, Noise XX secure channel, message router |
| [`src/platform/`](https://github.com/anishgoyal1108/EOS-Reimagined/tree/main/src/platform) | The *only* OS-specific code, behind a common header (`*_win32.cpp` / `*_linux.cpp`) |
| [`include/eos/`](https://github.com/anishgoyal1108/EOS-Reimagined/tree/main/include/eos) | Vendored EOS SDK headers — the ABI contract we implement against |
| [`tests/`](https://github.com/anishgoyal1108/EOS-Reimagined/tree/main/tests) | Unit, integration (loads the real artifact), trace, and export-surface suites |
| [`tools/`](https://github.com/anishgoyal1108/EOS-Reimagined/tree/main/tools) | [`inspect_game.py`](https://github.com/anishgoyal1108/EOS-Reimagined/blob/main/tools/inspect_game.py) (game-compatibility census), [`gen_stubs.py`](https://github.com/anishgoyal1108/EOS-Reimagined/blob/main/tools/gen_stubs.py) (generates the honest `EOS_NotImplemented` shells from the vendored headers), and [`alpha_runner.py`](../users/tracing.qmd#alpha_runnerpy-one-safe-diagnostic-game-run) (one safe, recoverable, traced game run) |
| [`wiki/`](https://github.com/anishgoyal1108/EOS-Reimagined/tree/main/wiki) | This site |

Build and test instructions live with the user docs — [Building from source](../users/building.qmd)
— because players build too. The short version: CMake ≥ 3.16, strict C++11,
[`scripts/test-all.sh`](https://github.com/anishgoyal1108/EOS-Reimagined/blob/main/scripts/test-all.sh)
runs everything on both targets.

## Reference material

- **Epic's official EOS SDK documentation** — the public behavioral reference we implement
  against: [EOS documentation](https://dev.epicgames.com/docs/epic-online-services) and the
  [C SDK API reference](https://dev.epicgames.com/docs/api-ref). When our spec and Epic's docs
  disagree, reality (the headers, and traced behavior of real games) wins — note it in the spec.
- **The vendored headers** in
  [`include/eos/`](https://github.com/anishgoyal1108/EOS-Reimagined/tree/main/include/eos) are
  the precise ABI: struct layouts, `ApiVersion` cutoffs, result codes. The headers are the law;
  the docs are the commentary.
- **[The internals section](internals/index.qmd)** — our own reverse-engineered spec of how the
  SDK (and the reference emulator) actually behaves on the wire and across ticks.
- **[ADR 0001](internals/adr/0001-authenticated-mesh-identity.qmd)** — the identity and
  secure-channel design every networked interface now rests on.

## Where help is most useful

1. **Game reports.** Run the [import census](../users/tracing.qmd#inspect_gamepy-will-this-game-even-load)
   against games you own — and play them with `EOSR_TRACE=lifecycle` — then attach the output to
   an issue. Which stubbed families real games actually touch is literally the prioritization
   data for what gets built next.
2. **Upgrade a stub into behavior.** Pick a family from
   [present but not functional](../users/roadmap.qmd#present-but-not-functional), read its spec
   page, implement it over the mesh or local state, and bring tests.
3. **Adversarial review.** Reading a merged interface against its spec and trying to break it is
   a first-class contribution here; the [manifest](internals/progress.qmd) shows the kind of
   findings that culture keeps producing.
